issue.title: fix(proxy): route Bedrock pass-through calls for AWS model ids the config does not list
issue.body:
## Handwritten 1-3 sentence description

Calling the Bedrock pass-through with a plain AWS model id, like the AWS SDK does, returned 400 "Invalid model name" on any proxy started with a config file. Now the proxy looks for a matching model first, and when there really is none it calls Bedrock directly with its own AWS credentials

[/stupid: What the PR adds](https://htmlpreview.github.io/?https://gist.githubusercontent.com/mateo-berri/2c897bb16881fb82378bba6a0abe7c69/raw/BerriAI-litellm-50737-stupid-purpose.html)

[/stupid: What breaks](https://htmlpreview.github.io/?https://gist.githubusercontent.com/mateo-berri/9a84922f9f82bbe1f89f07658d6100bd/raw/BerriAI-litellm-50737-stupid.html)

<details>
<summary>Details</summary>

## TLDR

Problem this solves:

- `/bedrock/model/<AWS model id>/...` answered 400 "Invalid model name" on any proxy with a config, for all four actions, boto3, and inference profile ARNs

How it solves it:

- A confirmed miss on a plain `model/<id>/<action>` path calls Bedrock directly with the proxy's AWS credentials
- Unpriced or non-chat ids, ids a deployment serves, provider budgets, failed lookups, non-ARN ids with a `/`, and a proxy without AWS credentials keep the 400
- Every Bedrock ARN in the model path is now percent-encoded

## User Flow

Before: the AWS SDK gets a 400 through the proxy for any model the config does not list

1. The proxy admin starts the proxy with a `config.yaml` and AWS credentials in its environment
2. The developer sends `POST http://localhost:4000/bedrock/model/us.anthropic.claude-haiku-5-5/converse` with a virtual key, or the same call through boto3
3. The proxy answers 400 `allm_passthrough_route: Invalid model name passed in model=us.anthropic.claude-haiku-5-5`

After: the same call reaches Bedrock and comes back with the model's answer

1. The proxy admin starts the proxy the same way
2. The developer sends the same call
3. The proxy answers 200 with Bedrock's own response

If you're seeing a delay in your PR being merged, ping the LiteLLM Team on [Slack (#pr-review)](https://join.slack.com/t/litellmossslack/shared_invite/zt-3o7nkuyfr-p_kbNJj8taRfXGgQI1~YyA).

## Screenshots / Proof of Fix

Each 400 below is the proxy's "Invalid model name" error

| Case | Before (87be092af7) | After (2d50f10b1a) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| curl converse | 400 | 200, "ok" |
| curl, the other three actions | 400 on each | 200 on each |
| curl converse with an ARN | 400 | 200, "ok" |
| boto3, four calls and the ARN | 400 on each | "ok" on each |
| Key limited to gpt-4o-mini | 403 | 403 |
| Unpriced id or embedding model | 400 | 400 |
| ARN Bedrock answers 403 | 400 | 400 |
| Config model name `nova` | 200, "ok" | 200, "ok" |
| Id `nova` serves | 400 | 400 |
| Id `claude-profile` wraps | 400 | 400 |
| `custom-deployment` ARN | 200, UnknownOperation | 404, Model not found |
| Key spend after the calls | $0.00000114, `nova` only | $0.00004294 |
| No AWS credentials, 8 parallel calls | 8 x 400 in 0.29 s | 8 x 400 in 0.25 s |
| Bedrock API key only | 400 | 200, "Ok." |

<details>
<summary>Setup (config, proxy command, boto3 client)</summary>

Both legs ran on one machine, each as its own proxy with 2 uvicorn workers and its own database on one Postgres server, with the same `config.yaml` and the same AWS role credentials in the proxy's environment. Every call went to real Bedrock in us-west-2. The headline model is `us.anthropic.claude-haiku-5-5`, which the config does not list. The config lists `nova`, `claude-profile` (an application inference profile over nova-micro), and `custom-deployment` (a custom model deployment ARN that does not exist)

`config.yaml`:

```
model_list:
  - model_name: nova
    litellm_params:
      model: bedrock/us.amazon.nova-lite-v1:0
      aws_region_name: us-west-2
  - model_name: claude-profile
    litellm_params:
      model: bedrock/arn:aws:bedrock:us-west-2:<account-id>:application-inference-profile/r4probeprofile
      aws_region_name: us-west-2
    model_info:
      base_model: bedrock/us.amazon.nova-micro-v1:0
  - model_name: custom-deployment
    litellm_params:
      model: bedrock/arn:aws:bedrock:us-west-2:<account-id>:custom-model-deployment/r4probe00000
      aws_region_name: us-west-2
litellm_settings:
  bedrock_request_metadata_fields:
    - user_api_key_team_alias
general_settings:
  master_key: os.environ/LITELLM_MASTER_KEY
  database_url: os.environ/DATABASE_URL
```

Env vars by name: `LITELLM_MASTER_KEY`, `DATABASE_URL`, `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`, `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`, `AWS_SESSION_TOKEN`, `AWS_REGION_NAME=us-west-2`. The boto3 client also reads `PORT`, `KEY`, and `ARN`

```
python litellm/proxy/proxy_cli.py --config config.yaml --port $PORT --num_workers 2
```

The boto3 client, pointed at the proxy with the virtual key as a bearer token:

```
import os, boto3, json
from botocore import UNSIGNED
from botocore.config import Config
c = boto3.client("bedrock-runtime", region_name="us-west-2", endpoint_url=f"http://127.0.0.1:{os.environ['PORT']}/bedrock", config=Config(signature_version=UNSIGNED))
c.meta.events.register("before-send.*.*", lambda request, **kw: request.headers.__setitem__("Authorization", f"Bearer {os.environ['KEY']}"))
m = "us.anthropic.claude-haiku-5-5"
msgs = [{"role":"user","content":[{"text":"Reply with the single word ok."}]}]
body = json.dumps({"anthropic_version":"bedrock-2023-05-31","max_tokens":16,"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Reply with the single word ok."}]})
calls = {
 "converse": lambda: c.converse(modelId=m, messages=msgs, inferenceConfig={"maxTokens":16})["output"]["message"]["content"][0]["text"],
 "converse_stream": lambda: "".join(e.get("contentBlockDelta",{}).get("delta",{}).get("text","") for e in c.converse_stream(modelId=m, messages=msgs, inferenceConfig={"maxTokens":16})["stream"]),
 "invoke_model": lambda: json.loads(c.invoke_model(modelId=m, body=body)["body"].read())["content"][0]["text"],
 "invoke_model_with_response_stream": lambda: "".join(json.loads(e["chunk"]["bytes"]).get("delta",{}).get("text","") for e in c.invoke_model_with_response_stream(modelId=m, body=body)["body"] if "chunk" in e),
}
arn = os.environ["ARN"]
calls["converse_with_arn"] = lambda: c.converse(modelId=arn, messages=msgs, inferenceConfig={"maxTokens":16})["output"]["message"]["content"][0]["text"]
for name, fn in calls.items():
    try: print(f"boto3 {name}: OK {fn()!r}")
    except Exception as e: print(f"boto3 {name}: {type(e).__name__} {str(e)[:200]}")
```

</details>

### Live risk run (2d50f10b1a against 87be092af7)

<details>
<summary>Breaking, backward incompatible, regression risk, dependency graph, not verified</summary>

Five proxy setups ran the same requests on both sides, each with 2 workers and a recorder in front of real Bedrock, plus two proxies sharing one database for the replica cases. Separate head checks covered a proxy with provider budgets, a burst of 60 unknown ids before a priced one, and a Bedrock 403 on both stream routes. Every difference is one the Decisions or Caveats below name

#### Breaking

None found. Every request that got a real Bedrock answer on the base gets the same answer on the head with the same request sent to Bedrock, and every key or team model limit still answers 403

#### Backward incompatible

- An unconfigured AWS id that litellm has a Bedrock chat price for, called with a key that has no model list or `all-proxy-models`, now gets Bedrock's 200 on the proxy's credentials where it got 400. This is the fix and the Severe caveat, and it waits on a maintainer's signoff
- On a `bedrock/*` wildcard proxy in us-east-1, a us-west-2 inference profile ARN now gets Bedrock's 400 after the router's 3 tries, where it got a 200 whose body was an UnknownOperationException. Listed under ARN model ids in Decisions, waiting on the same signoff
- A configured deployment whose model is a custom-model-deployment ARN now reaches Bedrock on the pass-through, where it got a 200 whose body was an UnknownOperationException. A test ARN that does not exist now gets Bedrock's 404 "Model not found"

#### Regression risk

- A custom-model ARN with a colon in its base model id is percent-encoded on the same path, and the Bedrock OpenAI-compatible invoke path now encodes both ARN shapes. Only unit tests cover those, since the test account has no custom model
- The first direct call on each worker looks up the proxy's AWS credentials in a thread before calling Bedrock. That lookup shares the credential cache with the call only when the call's region is `AWS_REGION_NAME`, so a proxy that assumes a role may make one extra STS call per worker
- The 60 s memory of a confirmed miss is per worker, so for up to a minute a worker whose lookup budget is spent can call Bedrock directly with the proxy's credentials for an id another replica has just added as a deployment

#### Dependency graph

| Dependent | Reached by | State |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Read-through retry in `route_request` | every model route | verified live |
| `RegistryReadThrough.attempt` | every model route | verified live, unit tests |
| Confirmed-miss memory | guardrail and agent lookups too | unit tests |
| Cost map check | Bedrock pass-through | verified live |
| Provider budget check | Bedrock pass-through | verified live |
| Served-model check | Bedrock pass-through | verified live |
| Served check from `base_model` | Bedrock pass-through | verified live |
| Bedrock 403 to 400 | Bedrock pass-through | verified live |
| ARN encoding in `llm_passthrough_route` | Bedrock pass-through | verified live |
| `encode_bedrock_runtime_modelid_arn` | Bedrock pass-through config | verified live, profile and deployment ARNs |
| `encode_bedrock_runtime_modelid_arn` | Bedrock OpenAI-compatible invoke | unit tests only |
| Deployment added on another replica | Bedrock pass-through | verified live |
| Proxy with no AWS credentials | Bedrock pass-through | verified live, 400 both sides |
| Missing-credentials memory | Bedrock pass-through | verified live, timed |
| `proxy_has_bedrock_credentials` lookup | Bedrock pass-through | verified live, unit tests |
| Lock held only for the lookup | Bedrock pass-through | verified live, timed |
| Proxy with an `openai/*` wildcard | Bedrock pass-through | verified live, 200 both sides |

#### Not verified

- A configured custom-model ARN deployment through chat completions, since the test account has no custom model
- A proxy with more than 2 workers
- A proxy that assumes a role through `AWS_ROLE_NAME` on a direct call

</details>

<details>
<summary>Decisions</summary>

- Where the fix lives
  - The proxy's request routing calls Bedrock directly after the model lookup misses
  - We did not add the route to the router's model-optional list, since that skipped the lookup and added router retries to the direct call
- When the direct call is allowed
  - Only when the lookup confirms the model is missing and the path is exactly `model/<the key's model>/<action>`, where the action is converse, converse-stream, invoke, or invoke-with-response-stream
  - The id must be a Bedrock chat model with a price in litellm's cost map, so a typo or a made-up id keeps litellm's 400 with no call to AWS, and every direct call is billed at a real price. A Bedrock model new to AWS gets the direct call once its price is in the cost map
  - Embedding, image, and rerank models keep the 400, since the pass-through's spend logging only reads chat responses and would record no spend for them
  - A router with provider budgets (`provider_budget_config`) keeps the 400, since the direct call skips the router and so skips the budget check
  - A key alias that renamed the model, a guardrail path, or any other Bedrock API keeps the 400
  - An id with a `/` keeps the 400 unless it is an ARN, since AWS answers a bare path like `application-inference-profile/abc123` with a 200 that carries an UnknownOperationException
  - A database error keeps the 400. A confirmed miss is remembered for 60 s, so a lookup the per-worker budget skips inside that minute still calls Bedrock directly, and a later lookup that finds the model clears it
- Which credentials and region an unlisted model uses
  - The proxy's own AWS credentials, the same ones the no-config proxy and the wildcard path already use
  - The region in an ARN id, else the proxy's `AWS_REGION_NAME` or `AWS_REGION`, else us-west-2, as on a proxy with no config. No deployment serves the id, so there is no deployment region to use
  - A model the config routes (exact name, wildcard, or deployment model name) still uses that deployment's credentials and region, covered by a regression test
  - A deployment created on another replica is loaded by the lookup and keeps its own credentials
- An AWS id a configured deployment already serves
  - It keeps the 400, and the deployment's config model name works as before
  - A deployment serves the id when its model names the same base model once the region prefix, ARN, and route prefix come off. So a deployment for `us.anthropic.claude-haiku-5-5` also keeps the 400 for `anthropic.claude-haiku-5-5`, `global.anthropic.claude-haiku-5-5`, and the profile ARN
  - A deployment's `base_model` or `model_info.base_model` counts too, so an application inference profile deployment keeps the 400 for the model it wraps
  - The served models are cached until a deployment changes. Rebuilding them takes about 31 ms at 2,000 deployments, and a cached check takes about 0.002 ms
  - We did not send a served id direct, since that would skip the deployment's credentials, region, guardrails, and price
  - We did not route it to that deployment either. No route does that today, two model groups can list the same AWS id so the pick would be arbitrary, and a key would reach a deployment its model list does not name
- Which keys can make the direct call
  - Any key whose model list allows the id, including a key with no list or `all-proxy-models`, as the pass-through docs show with `Bearer sk-anything`
  - This is the Severe caveat below and waits on a maintainer's call between shipping as is, limiting the direct call to keys whose model list names the id or a wildcard, putting it behind an opt-in setting, or not shipping
  - We did not gate it on `pass_through_all_models`, since the docs scope that flag to SDK completion and embedding calls
- Bedrock errors on the direct call
  - A 403 from Bedrock answers the proxy's own 400 "Invalid model name", so a caller never sees the proxy's IAM role or account
  - Any other Bedrock error, like a 400 for a bad request body, passes through unchanged, as `bedrock/*` already does today
- ARN model ids
  - Every Bedrock ARN in the model path is percent-encoded, since AWS rejects a raw `/` there
  - That covers a custom model whose base model id has colons, like `custom-model/amazon.titan-text-express-v1:0:8k/<id>`, and a `custom-model-deployment` ARN
  - On a wildcard or no-config proxy, an ARN AWS does not know now answers Bedrock's 400 where it answered a 200 that carried an UnknownOperationException
- A proxy with no AWS credentials of its own
  - It keeps the 400 "Invalid model name", so a caller sees the same answer as before
  - After a credential lookup finds nothing, that worker answers the 400 for 60 s without looking again. Calls that arrive during a lookup wait for that lookup only, and once credentials are found each call goes to Bedrock on its own
  - A proxy whose only Bedrock credential is a Bedrock API key (`AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK`) counts as having credentials
  - A proxy with half an AWS setup, like an access key with no secret, answers Bedrock's credential error instead, so the operator sees the broken setup

</details>

## Type

🐛 Bug Fix

## Caveats (if any)

<!-- caveats round 4 of 4 -->

### Severe

- A key or team with no model list, or `all-proxy-models`, can now call any priced Bedrock chat model the proxy's AWS identity allows, billed to that account, on a proxy whose config lists only named models. No setting turns it off. Any wildcard model, even `openai/*`, already allows this, and model lists still limit it. Needs a maintainer's signoff before merge

### Medium

- An AWS id a configured deployment serves keeps the 400, since routing by AWS id would let a key reach a deployment its model list does not name
- The direct call uses the proxy's region, never a deployment's, so an EU-only config can send an unlisted model's prompt to us-west-2 unless the proxy sets `AWS_REGION_NAME`
- A deployment another replica just added under a different name stops the direct call here only after the next model refresh, or 60 s after a confirmed miss. A shorter memory sends random names to the database more often

### Low

- With no AWS credentials, each worker still looks for them once a minute, with no slowdown measured here. Skipping it would change how every Bedrock call finds credentials
- Every model route shares the per-worker lookup budget, so a burst of new ids can delay finding a new deployment by up to 5 s. Changing that older budget here is not worth the risk
- Expired proxy credentials also show as "Invalid model name" on a direct call, since telling that 403 apart would show callers the proxy's credential state
- A pre-existing gap went to security engineering

## Final Attestation

- [x] The tests check the right things, including the edge cases, and regressions in the respective real-world customer use-cases are not possible after this PR

</details>

issue.title: fix(streaming): keep Azure prompt_filter_results and finish-chunk content_filter_results in chat streams
issue.body:
When you stream a chat completion from an Azure OpenAI deployment through litellm, Azure's content filter verdict on the prompt never reaches you, and the last chunk loses the verdict Azure puts on its choice. Non-streaming calls already pass the prompt verdict on

This PR carries both through the stream. Azure sends the prompt verdict on an empty chunk before any text, so litellm now puts it on the first chunk the client gets, or keeps it on that empty chunk when the caller asked for usage chunks. It works through the proxy too, now that #49398 keeps extra chunk fields on the proxy's fast streaming path

<details>
<summary>Original</summary>

## TLDR

Problem this solves:

- Streamed Azure chats drop `prompt_filter_results`
- The finish chunk drops its `content_filter_results`
- Non-streaming calls already keep `prompt_filter_results`

How it solves it:

- Fields on Azure's empty first chunk move to the first chunk with a choice
- A caller who asked for `include_usage` gets them on Azure's own empty chunk
- The finish chunk copies the upstream choice's extra fields

Intentional product change: streamed Azure chats now carry `prompt_filter_results` and the finish chunk's `content_filter_results`, which clients never got before

<details>
<summary>Decisions</summary>

- Move the fields forward instead of sending Azure's `"choices": []` chunk to every caller
  - A caller who never asked for usage chunks does not expect an empty-choice chunk, and code that reads `chunk.choices[0]` would crash on it
  - Alternatives: always send the empty chunk (matches Azure byte for byte, breaks those clients), or keep dropping it (the bug)
- A caller who set `stream_options.include_usage` already gets empty-choice chunks, so the fields stay on Azure's own empty chunk, exactly as Azure sends it
- When the proxy added `include_usage` itself, it drops its empty chunks, so the fields move forward like the no-usage case
- Only empty chunks before the first chunk sent are held. Later usage-only chunks keep today's handling
- A field the first chunk already has wins over a held one, and null values are never held
- Carry every non-OpenAI top-level field, the same rule chunks with choices already follow, instead of naming `prompt_filter_results`
  - Alternative: an Azure-only list, which misses the next field Azure adds
- The finish chunk copies the upstream choice's extra fields (minus `message`), the same rule content chunks already follow
  - Only when upstream and litellm each have one choice with the same index, since an n>1 stream can build one choice's finish chunk while another choice's chunk is in hand, and copying then put that other choice's fields on it
  - Null values are skipped, so a finish chunk is the same as before when the upstream field is null
  - vLLM's `token_ids` are skipped, since the vLLM stream code already places them per chunk and strips them under post-call rules

</details>

## User Flow

Before: a developer streaming from an Azure deployment never sees Azure's prompt filter verdict

1. They send POST https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions with `"stream": true` to an Azure model
2. No chunk carries `prompt_filter_results`, though Azure sent it before any text
3. The last chunk, with `"finish_reason": "stop"`, has no `content_filter_results`

After: the same stream carries both verdicts

1. They send the same POST https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions with `"stream": true`
2. The first chunk carries `prompt_filter_results`, or with `stream_options.include_usage` the leading `"choices": []` chunk does, as from Azure
3. The last chunk keeps `content_filter_results`

## Relevant issues

Builds on #49398, which keeps extra chunk fields on the proxy's fast streaming path

## Pre-Submission checklist

**Please complete all items before asking a LiteLLM maintainer to review your PR**

- [x] I have added meaningful tests
- [x] The handful of test files covering my change pass locally, e.g. `uv run pytest tests/unit/<your_test_file>.py -v`. Leave the suites (`make test-unit-*`, `make test-unit`) to CI: it finishes in ~15 minutes where a laptop takes an hour or more
- [ ] My PR passes all required CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, schema.d.ts sync check, etc.)
- [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem

issue.title: fix(responses): report the client's model name on WebSocket events, retrieve, and non-streamed fallbacks
issue.body:
When a client calls the proxy by an alias, most responses already come back with that alias as `model`. Three places still showed the backend's own model name instead: WebSocket mode on /v1/responses, GET and cancel on /v1/responses/{id}, and a non-streamed request that fell back to another model group

This PR makes those three report the same name the streamed paths already report, so a client sees one model name for one call no matter how it makes it. Billing and logs still see the provider's model

<details>
<summary>Details</summary>

## TLDR

Problem this solves:

- WebSocket events report the backend model, not the client's alias
- GET and cancel on a stored response report the backend model, streamed GET included
- Non-streamed fallbacks report the backend model, streamed ones the fallback group

How it solves it:

- WebSocket relays put the client's model on events sent to the client
- GET and cancel report the model group the response id points at, on every event of a streamed GET too
- Non-streamed fallbacks report the fallback group, same as streaming
- Billing and logs keep the provider's model

## User Flow

Before: an app that calls the proxy by alias sees a different model name depending on how it calls

1. The app opens ws://litellm-domain/v1/responses and sends `response.create` with `"model": "oai-alias"`. Every event's `response.model` is `gpt-5.4-mini-2026-03-17`
2. It sends POST https://litellm-domain/v1/responses with `"model": "oai-alias"` and `"store": true` and gets `"model": "oai-alias"`. Then GET https://litellm-domain/v1/responses/{id} shows `"model": "gpt-5.4-mini-2026-03-17"`, and so does every event of GET https://litellm-domain/v1/responses/{id}?stream=true
3. It sends POST /v1/responses or /v1/chat/completions to `broken-primary`, which is down and falls back to `gpt-mini`. The streamed call reports `gpt-mini` and the non-streamed one reports `gpt-5.4-mini-2026-03-17`

After: the same app sees the name it asked for, or the fallback group, everywhere

1. The app opens ws://litellm-domain/v1/responses and sends `response.create` with `"model": "oai-alias"`. Every event's `response.model` is `oai-alias`
2. It sends POST https://litellm-domain/v1/responses with `"model": "oai-alias"` and `"store": true` and gets `"model": "oai-alias"`. Then GET https://litellm-domain/v1/responses/{id} shows `"model": "oai-alias"` too, and so does every event of GET https://litellm-domain/v1/responses/{id}?stream=true
3. It sends POST /v1/responses or /v1/chat/completions to `broken-primary`, which is down and falls back to `gpt-mini`. The streamed and non-streamed calls both report `gpt-mini`

<details>
<summary>Decisions</summary>

1. A non-streamed fallback reports the fallback group (`gpt-mini`), the name streaming already reports. The other options were the alias the client asked for, which hides that a fallback happened, and the backend name, which is today's bug. When the router sets no group header, the response is left as is
2. GET and cancel report the model group of the deployment the response id points at, since nothing stores the name used at create time. So a response created through a team alias or `model_group_alias` comes back with the group name, not the alias. A team model reports its public name instead of its internal routing key, and a wildcard deployment keeps the provider model so a GET never says `openai/*`
3. GET and cancel keep the provider model when the request asks for raw model names, and for a model group that a complexity router set to return raw model names can pick (a tier or its default model), since a GET can't tell whether that router picked the response. Other groups on the same proxy still get their group name. The other option was skipping every group once any such router exists, which QA showed hides the fix on those proxies
4. Spend rows and the standard logging payload keep the provider's model. GET and cancel rename a copy, and WebSocket renames only the frame sent to the client, so turn history keeps it too. A streamed GET renames each event the way a streamed create already does, so the read's own log entry, which carries no cost, shows the group like a streamed create's shows the alias, while the background job's bill keeps the provider's model. A non-streamed fallback renames the response in place like the existing alias rename, so a custom callback reading `response_obj.model` now sees the fallback group, the same way it already saw the alias when no fallback ran
5. On the WebSocket relay for providers without native WebSocket support, a frame that names its own model reports that model, since the relay routes on it
6. A WebSocket session is not renamed to a fallback group. The relay handles a failed backend connect itself, so no router fallback runs there
7. A non-streamed fallback into an Azure Model Router, or into a complexity router set to return raw model names, keeps the model that answered, since a direct request to that group does. The other option was the router's group name, which overrides that operator setting only when a fallback ran
8. The `x-litellm-model-group` header on GET still shows the deployment id instead of the group name. That has the same root cause as retry policies not applying to GET and DELETE, and is tracked separately

</details>

<details>
<summary>Integration test expectations this PR changes</summary>

- `routing/test_fallback_retry_header_contracts.py`, the two client fallback cells: the non-streamed chat call falls back, so the body names the fallback group instead of its upstream model
- `routing/test_observed_routing.py`, every non-streamed 200 case: each one falls back, so the body names the group that answered (`big`, `safe`, `general`, or `primary` after order failover) like the streamed cases already did
- `providers/test_responses_lifecycle_wire.py`, retrieve after create, retrieve after a stream, retrieve with query params (plain and streamed), and cancel: the body and the streamed events name the model group the response id points at, as create already did
- `authorization/test_responses_id_ownership.py`, retrieve, cancel, and retrieve of a follow-up: same reason
- `streaming/test_stream_contracts.py`, the non-streamed /v1/messages and /v1/responses fallback cells: the body names the fallback group instead of its upstream model

</details>

<details>
<summary>Live A/B against the merge base (/live-pr-risk)</summary>

Both legs ran on one box with Postgres, 2 workers each, the same config and the same 59 cells, with a recording proxy in front of OpenAI and a custom callback that logs what each hook receives. The outbound requests and their count match on both legs, and so do the spend rows (call type, model, model group, provider, status, spend). Every difference in what the client sees is one this PR names

The same cells on this branch merged into main at c98641fd5a give the same results as the branch alone. The unit tests that reach the changed code also pass on this branch merged into main at cfb77ecc3a, and again after merging main at 43c07a0f12. On that merge one WebSocket admission test fails when xdist runs it in a new order. It fails the same way alone on main, because `websockets.exceptions` is never imported there

The integration groups that reach this code (routing, providers, management, accounting) pass on this branch. The only red is a Vertex Model Garden header case that times out on the merge base too and passed when run again here

### Breaking

None found

### Backward incompatible

- A non-streamed fallback on /v1/chat/completions, /v1/responses, and /v1/messages returns the fallback group as `model` where it returned the provider's model. This is the fix Mateo asked for in the ticket behind this PR
- A key alias whose group fails over to another deployment in the same group (`my-ordered` to `ordered`) now reports `ordered`, the name the streamed call already reported. Same ticket
- A custom callback reading `response_obj.model` in `async_post_call_success_hook` or `async_log_success_event` sees the fallback group after a non-streamed fallback. The standard logging payload and spend rows keep the provider's model. Same ticket, decision 4

### Regression risk

- A client that compares `model` on a fallback response with the provider's model name now gets the group name. Nothing in the repo does this
- The streamed fallback paths are unchanged, so a streamed fallback into a raw-name complexity router still reports the router's group on both legs while the non-streamed one keeps the served model. That split already existed at the merge base

### Dependency graph

| Dependent | Status |
| --- | --- |
| Non-streamed chat, responses, messages fallback | verified live |
| Fallback into raw-name complexity router | verified live |
| Fallback into Azure Model Router | unit test only |
| Text completion, embeddings, compact | verified live, unchanged |
| GET and cancel, alias, team, wildcard | verified live |
| GET for a group a raw-name router picks | verified live, unchanged |
| Streamed GET of a background response | verified live, changed |
| WebSocket, native and relay | verified live |
| WebSocket, key alias, team, wildcard, multi-turn | verified live |
| WebSocket into raw-name router | verified live, unchanged |
| WebSocket bad model, hostile metadata | verified live, unchanged |
| Streamed fallbacks | verified live, unchanged |
| Spend rows, logging payload | verified live, unchanged |
| Callback `response_obj.model` | verified live, changed |
| Outbound request to OpenAI | verified live, unchanged |

### Not verified

- A non-streamed fallback into an Azure Model Router group. None of the QA Azure resources has a model-router deployment, so a unit test covers it
- WebSocket fallback to another group. The relay fails over to nothing on both legs, since it never runs router fallbacks
- The log entry of a streamed GET, which carries no cost, now names the group. That comes from reading the logging code, not from a live callback

</details>

## Screenshots / Proof of Fix

Last updated: c581a51fc4. QA ran on 572f26b0cd. Changes since QA: one integration test now expects the fallback group, and a merge of main at 43c07a0f12 whose only conflict was the import list in `litellm/responses/main.py`, resolved by keeping both sides. Proof remains valid because neither commit changes this PR's product code. Verification: the changed test passes on 1171ef758e and its old expectation passes on the merge base, and `make check` and the unit tests that reach the changed code pass on the merge

```python
import asyncio, json, sys
import websockets

async def main() -> None:
    base, key, model = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2], sys.argv[3]
    async with websockets.connect(f"{base}/v1/responses", additional_headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {key}"}) as ws:
        await ws.send(json.dumps({"type": "response.create", "model": model, "input": "Reply with ok"}))
        seen = []
        while True:
            event = json.loads(await ws.recv())
            if "response" in event:
                seen.append(f"{event['type']}={event['response'].get('model')}")
            if event["type"] in ("response.completed", "response.failed", "error"):
                break
        print(f"websocket requested {model}: " + ", ".join(seen))

asyncio.run(main())
```

issue.title: fix(proxy): count xAI grok tokens with xAI's tokenizer
issue.body:
## Handwritten 1-3 sentence description

Token counts for grok models used OpenAI's tokenizer, so a count could be 99% under or 84% over what xAI or Azure then billed. Grok models served by xAI now count with xAI's own tokenizer and come within about 3% of the bill, and an admin can opt Azure-hosted grok into the same count. Each grok model's fixed prompt overhead is stored in the model cost map, so a new grok model needs its overhead measured there

<details>
<summary>Details</summary>

## TLDR

Problem this solves:

- grok token counts used OpenAI's tokenizer, off by up to 84%
- Azure-hosted grok had no way to get an accurate count

How it solves it:

- `xai/` deployments count with xAI's `/v1/tokenize-text`
- The cost map stores each grok model's fixed prompt overhead
- Azure grok counts through xAI only when its admin opts in

## User Flow

Before: a developer who sizes a grok request with count_tokens gets a number far from what the request then bills

1. They send POST https://litellm-domain/v1/messages/count_tokens with `"model": "grok-4.7"` and a user message saying "hi"
2. It returns `{"input_tokens": 8, "litellm_count_source": "local_estimate"}`
3. They send the same body to POST https://litellm-domain/v1/messages
4. `usage` bills 1243 input tokens (91 input plus 1152 cache read), so the count was 99% low

After: the same count matches what the request bills

1. They send POST https://litellm-domain/v1/messages/count_tokens with `"model": "grok-4.7"` and a user message saying "hi"
2. It returns `{"input_tokens": 1243, "litellm_count_source": "provider"}`
3. They send the same body to POST https://litellm-domain/v1/messages
4. `usage` bills 1243 input tokens, the same as the count. On an Azure grok model whose admin set `token_count_model` to an xAI model, a Chinese report counts 559 against 562 billed, where main counts 1034

## Pre-Submission checklist

**Please complete all items before asking a LiteLLM maintainer to review your PR**

- [x] I have added meaningful tests
- [x] The handful of test files covering my change pass locally, e.g. `uv run pytest tests/unit/<your_test_file>.py -v`. Leave the suites (`make test-unit-*`, `make test-unit`) to CI: it finishes in ~15 minutes where a laptop takes an hour or more
- [ ] My PR passes all required CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, schema.d.ts sync check, etc.)
- [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem
- [ ] Every automated review on my PR's latest commit has finished, and I have addressed or replied to each of its findings before requesting a maintainer review

## Delays in PR merge?

If you're seeing a delay in your PR being merged, ping the LiteLLM Team on [Slack (#pr-review)](https://join.slack.com/t/litellmossslack/shared_invite/zt-3o7nkuyfr-p_kbNJj8taRfXGgQI1~YyA).

## Screenshots / Proof of Fix

Both legs ran one proxy with 2 uvicorn workers and no database, booted from the tree under test with `PYTHON_DOTENV_DISABLED=1 LITELLM_LOCAL_MODEL_COST_MAP=True litellm --config config.yaml --port <random port> --num_workers 2 --timeout_worker_healthcheck 60`, with `LITELLM_MASTER_KEY`, `XAI_API_KEY`, `AZURE_FOUNDRY_API_BASE` and `AZURE_FOUNDRY_API_KEY` set, and real xAI and Azure AI Foundry calls. The local map flag makes each proxy read its own tree's cost map. `$PROXY` is that leg's `http://127.0.0.1:<port>`, and every curl also sends `-H "Authorization: Bearer $LITELLM_MASTER_KEY" -H 'Content-Type: application/json'`. The [gist](https://gist.github.com/mateo-berri/d035bf4353208f1c750069a3f9b128a3) has the leg and stall scripts exactly as run, the five request bodies, and the raw count_tokens and usage JSON of every table row

<details>

The blocks below run in order in one shell from a clone of the gist. Each model counts "What is the weather in Paris?" on /v1/messages/count_tokens and /v1/responses/input_tokens, with and without a `get_weather` tool, then sends the same body to /v1/messages or /v1/responses

```
U=$PROXY
H=(-H "Authorization: Bearer $LITELLM_MASTER_KEY" -H 'Content-Type: application/json')
RAW=raw.log
BODIES=.
pair() {
  local label=$1 body=$2 count_route=$3 bill_route=$4 bill_body=$5
  local count=$(curl -s $U$count_route $H -d "$body")
  local usage=$(curl -s $U$bill_route $H -d "$bill_body" | jq -c .usage)
  print -r -- "$label count_tokens=$count usage=$usage" >> $RAW
  local c=$(print -r -- $count | jq .input_tokens)
  local b=$(print -r -- $usage | jq '.input_tokens + (.cache_read_input_tokens // 0) + (.cache_creation_input_tokens // 0)')
  printf "%-44s %8s %8s %+7.1f%% %s\n" $label $c $b $(( (c - b) * 100.0 / b )) $(print -r -- $count | jq -r '.litellm_count_source // "-"')
}

MSG_TOOL='{"name":"get_weather","description":"Get the current weather for a city","input_schema":{"type":"object","properties":{"city":{"type":"string","description":"City name"}},"required":["city"]}}'
RESP_TOOL='{"type":"function","name":"get_weather","description":"Get the current weather for a city","parameters":{"type":"object","properties":{"city":{"type":"string","description":"City name"}},"required":["city"]}}'
print "== request kinds =="
printf "%-44s %8s %8s %8s %s\n" case count billed diff source
for model in grok-4.3 grok-4-1 grok-4-1-no-xai-count grok-4.7; do
  for tools in none weather; do
    t=$([[ $tools == none ]] && print '[]' || print "[$MSG_TOOL]")
    body=$(jq -nc --arg m "$model" --argjson t "$t" '{model:$m,max_tokens:1,messages:[{role:"user",content:"What is the weather in Paris?"}]} + (if ($t|length) > 0 then {tools:$t} else {} end)')
    pair "$model messages tools=$tools" "$body" /v1/messages/count_tokens /v1/messages "$body"
    rt=$([[ $tools == none ]] && print '[]' || print "[$RESP_TOOL]")
    rbody=$(jq -nc --arg m "$model" --argjson t "$rt" '{model:$m,input:"What is the weather in Paris?"} + (if ($t|length) > 0 then {tools:$t} else {} end)')
    pair "$model responses tools=$tools" "$rbody" /v1/responses/input_tokens /v1/responses "$(print -r -- $rbody | jq -c '. + {max_output_tokens:16}')"
  done
done
```

<details>
<summary>Decisions</summary>

- What text xAI counts: the prompt as grok's chat template renders it (`Human: hi<|separator|>\n\n` per turn, consecutive same-role messages joined with a newline). Content-only text missed the per-turn labels, and the public grok-1 and grok-2 tokenizers, o200k and cl100k all missed grok-4's counts
- The fixed overhead every request bills on top of the rendered prompt (1238 tokens on grok-4.7 and 180 on grok-4.20) is measured per model and stored in the cost map as `token_count_framing`, and the proxy adds it to counts from counters that leave it out. The alternatives were hardcoding it in the counter or having the counter read the cost map, which would skip the admin's own `model_info.token_count_framing` override
- Main already stores this overhead for Azure grok-4-1-fast-reasoning and grok-4.3, split by tools and Responses, and measured it against the local estimate. The xAI count adds the value for the request's kind from those same rows, so one-message prompts on those models count 3 tokens under. The alternatives were a second set of cost map keys for the xAI count, or raising main's values by 3, which would put the local estimate 3 over
- Azure grok counts through xAI only when the admin sets `model_info.token_count_model` to an xAI model and the proxy has `XAI_API_KEY`. A `token_count_model` that comes from the cost map is ignored, so a map update never sends prompts to a second provider. The alternative was to honor map defaults, which would turn xAI counting on for every Azure grok deployment without anyone asking. Only Azure grok-4-1-fast-reasoning has a measured overhead, so other Azure grok models need `model_info.token_count_framing` set by hand
- A deployment that is not xAI never sends its own key or api_base to xAI. The count uses `XAI_API_KEY` and `XAI_API_BASE` instead
- Requests with image parts, Gemini `contents`, or a body the Anthropic adapter cannot translate fall back to the local estimate. Counting only their text with xAI would silently drop the image tokens
- On grok-4-1 and grok-4.3, xAI gets the tools the way main's chat template renders them, one JSON line per function, because main's tool overhead already covers the rest of the tool turn. Sending the whole OpenAI tool list as a system turn counted that wrapper twice and came 3% to 11% high on the weather tool probes. Other grok models have no known template, so their tools go as a JSON system turn ahead of the conversation. The system, tool and user probe on grok-4.7 comes 1.1% low that way, where leaving tools out missed about 90 tokens
- On Azure Responses, a function tool with no `strict` goes to xAI as strict, because Azure bills an unset strict like true and main's local estimate already counts it that way. Leaving it out counted the weather tool 4 more tokens under
- xAI errors come back with xAI's status, so a 503 or a timeout reaches the client. A 400 or 404 still falls back to the estimate plus overhead when no count model is configured, which is the existing rule for every provider counter, and xAI answers a wrong key with 400, so a wrong key gets the estimate. Falling back on every error would hide an xAI outage behind the local estimate this PR replaces, with nothing to tell the client
- A grok model with no known overhead (no cost map row and no `model_info.token_count_framing`) keeps the local estimate and never calls xAI. When its admin opted in with `token_count_model`, the proxy logs a warning that names `model_info.token_count_framing`. Sending xAI's count without the overhead would come back short by 150 to 1240 tokens with `provider` as its source, and a default of 0 would hide the same gap
- `token_count_model.model` takes the name with or without the `xai/` prefix, so `xai/grok-4-1-fast-reasoning` counts the same as `grok-4-1-fast-reasoning`. Without that the prefixed name reached xAI as `xai/xai/...` and failed
- `litellm.acount_tokens` in the Python SDK adds the same overhead, and the tool overhead when the request sends tools, so the SDK and the proxy give the same number. Before that the SDK counted grok-4.3 with the weather tool 29 tokens under the proxy
- An `xai/` deployment with no key of its own and no `XAI_API_KEY` (an OAuth deployment) keeps the local estimate. An Azure deployment that opted in to xAI counting without `XAI_API_KEY` answers 401 naming the env var, because the admin asked for xAI's count
- xAI's reply lists every token with its text and has no option to leave the strings out, so a 139k token prompt comes back as about 14 MB. The count is the number of `"token_id":` keys in the raw reply, and a reply with none answers 502. In xAI's compact JSON an unescaped quote can only open a key, because a quote inside a token's text arrives as `\"`, and a test counts token texts that spell the key. Parsing the reply into a typed model held the worker's event loop for 1.9 s on a 542k token count. A worker thread does not help because the parse holds the GIL, and an untyped parse still builds every token object. With the byte count, the slowest health check during a 551k token count took 3 ms
- The tokenize-text call stops waiting after 30 seconds, the same as Bedrock's count calls. Without it the call used the 600 second completion default, so a hung xAI call held count_tokens for 10 minutes

</details>

## Type

🐛 Bug Fix

## Caveats (if any)

<!-- caveats round 1 of 4 -->

### Medium

- The docs count_tokens page does not cover xAI counting yet

### Low

- Azure grok tool turns count about 23% under, same as main
- Released proxies add this map's overhead to their old estimate
  - grok-4.7 gets closer, grok-4.20 Chinese text gets further off
- xAI 5xx errors and timeouts reach the client, like other counters

## Final Attestation

- [x] The tests check the right things, including the edge cases, and regressions in the respective real-world customer use-cases are not possible after this PR

</details>

issue.title: fix(responses): stop the background stream when a polling response is cancelled
issue.body:
With polling via cache on, cancelling a background response only flipped its status in Redis. The model call kept running and billing, its last write put the response back to completed, and the key's parallel slot stayed taken until the call finished

Now the background task reads the stored state once a second and stops the model call when it reads cancelled or the response is gone, on any pod. State writes skip a cancelled response, so the cancel sticks

A cancel before the model answers, or a client hangup during keepalive pings on any of the three routes, frees the slot at once and logs a failure row

<details>
<summary>Original</summary>

## TLDR

Problem this solves:

- A cancelled polling response shows as completed a few seconds later
- The model call keeps running and billing after a cancel or a delete
- A cancel before the model answered kept the key's parallel slot

How it solves it:

- The background task stops its stream once it reads cancelled or gone
- State writes skip a response that is already cancelled, in one Redis step
- A cancel before the model answers, or a client hangup during keepalive pings on any route, frees the slot and logs a failure row

## User Flow

Before, a developer cancels a background response, but it finishes anyway and shows as completed

1. They send POST https://litellm-domain/v1/responses with `"background": true` and get back `"id": "litellm_poll_<uuid>"` with `"status": "queued"`
2. They send POST https://litellm-domain/v1/responses/litellm_poll_<uuid>/cancel and get back `"status": "cancelled"`
3. The model keeps generating, and the provider bills the whole answer
4. 10 seconds later, GET https://litellm-domain/v1/responses/litellm_poll_<uuid> returns `"status": "completed"` with the full output

After, the same cancel stops the model call, and the response stays cancelled

1. They send POST https://litellm-domain/v1/responses with `"background": true` and get back `"id": "litellm_poll_<uuid>"` with `"status": "queued"`
2. They send POST https://litellm-domain/v1/responses/litellm_poll_<uuid>/cancel and get back `"status": "cancelled"`, even when another gateway instance runs the call
3. About a second later the gateway closes the model call, so the provider stops generating
4. 10 seconds later, GET https://litellm-domain/v1/responses/litellm_poll_<uuid> still returns `"status": "cancelled"`

## Decisions

<details>
<summary>Choices made and the alternatives turned down</summary>

1. Every state write goes through a small Lua script that sets the key only when it exists and its status is not cancelled. The read and the merge of fields stay in Python
   - WATCH/MULTI was turned down. It needs a dedicated connection and a retry loop for every partial flush of a stream
   - A separate cancel-marker key was turned down. Every read of a response would need to merge a second key, and the two keys' TTLs would have to stay in step
   - A plain SET fallback for a Redis that refuses EVAL was turned down. It would bring the overwrite back, and the parallel request limiter already needs EVAL
2. The background task reads the state every 1 second, which is a module constant
   - A shorter interval adds a Redis read per second for every running background response
   - A longer one lets more tokens bill after a cancel
3. The task polls the stored state instead of listening on Redis pub/sub
   - Pub/sub loses a message when nobody is subscribed at that moment, e.g. during a worker restart or a dropped connection
   - A poll always reads the stored state, so a cancel is never missed, and it needs no new channel
4. The state is now written with `status` as its first field, so the script and the background task compare a fixed prefix of the stored value with GETRANGE instead of decoding it. Each write and each read costs the same whatever the response size
   - Decoding the stored JSON inside Lua was turned down. It took 0.3 ms to 10.7 ms per write on long responses, and Redis runs nothing else while a script runs
   - The value keeps its double encoding (a JSON string inside a JSON string), so responses that older pods stored still read back. During a rolling deploy, a background task still running on an older pod ignores a cancel, and its last write sets the response back to completed. A new pod also misses a cancel that an older pod writes while the response is still `queued`
5. A cancel that lands before the model answers is reported once as a client disconnect (HTTP 499) through the proxy's failure hooks, the same path a client that hangs up takes. That gives the key's parallel slot and budget reservation back and writes a failure row to the spend logs
   - Releasing the parallel slot directly was turned down. It writes no spend row, so the key owner could not see the cancelled call
   - Once the stream has started, its own disconnect cleanup settles the call, so the task does not report it a second time
6. DELETE stops the call too. The background task stops when the stored response is missing, not only when it reads cancelled
   - Stopping only on cancelled was turned down. A deleted response cannot be read anymore, so a call that keeps running only bills tokens nobody gets
7. A failed state read keeps the stream running and logs a warning. Stopping the call on a read error would cancel every running background response during a Redis blip
8. A failed state write logs an error and the stream goes on, like the old write path, which never raised
9. A background response cancelled while the proxy is still sending keepalive pings, before the model's first token, reports one client disconnect (HTTP 499) through the failure hooks, as Decision 5 does. The fix sits in the shared keepalive wrapper, so a client that drops a keepalive stream before its first token on chat completions, /v1/messages or /v1/responses now gets its parallel slot back too
   - When the call has already failed by the time the reader leaves, that failure is reported instead of a disconnect, so a 429 or 500 is not logged as a hangup
   - When the model has already answered by the time the reader leaves, nothing is reported, since the answered stream's own disconnect cleanup settles the call, as in Decision 5
   - Fixing only the polling path was turned down. Those three routes leaked the slot the same way
   - Pass-through and RAG streams give the wrapper no failure callback, so a hangup during their pings works as it did before. Wiring them goes in its own change
10. A cut call bills LiteLLM's own prompt token count, the same as a client that hangs up mid-stream on any route
   - Billing the provider's input count from its first stream event (Anthropic's `message_start`) was turned down here. It changes disconnect billing on every route, so it goes in its own change
11. A cancel before the first token refunds the key's budget reservation to $0, matching a client that hangs up before the first token. Its spend row is a $0 failure, so the budget and the logs agree
   - Charging the estimated input cost, as a mid-stream hangup does, was turned down. The budget would then say a cost the $0 spend row does not show
   - Logs and callbacks show the cancel as "client disconnected", since that is the proxy's one name for a call the caller stopped
12. A `ttl` that is not a number (null or "1h") falls back to the cache's default ttl, as the old write path did
   - Rejecting it at config load was turned down. Configs that boot today would stop booting

</details>

## Pre-Submission checklist

**Please complete all items before asking a LiteLLM maintainer to review your PR**

- [x] I have added meaningful tests
- [x] The handful of test files covering my change pass locally, e.g. `uv run pytest tests/unit/<your_test_file>.py -v`. Leave the suites (`make test-unit-*`, `make test-unit`) to CI: it finishes in ~15 minutes where a laptop takes an hour or more
- [ ] My PR passes all required CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, schema.d.ts sync check, etc.)
- [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem
- [ ] Every automated review on my PR's latest commit has finished, and I have addressed or replied to each of its findings before requesting a maintainer review

## Delays in PR merge?

If you're seeing a delay in your PR being merged, ping the LiteLLM Team on [Slack (#pr-review)](https://join.slack.com/t/litellmossslack/shared_invite/zt-3o7nkuyfr-p_kbNJj8taRfXGgQI1~YyA).

## Screenshots / Proof of Fix

| Case | Before (3b9a59348f) | After (7b3e1f7bbf) |
|---|---|---|
| No cancel | completed | completed |
| Early cancel, +20 s | completed | cancelled |
| Mid-stream cancel, +20 s | completed, 6610 chars | cancelled, 284 chars |
| One-slot key, early cancel, +3 s | 429 | 200 |
| One-slot key, mid-stream cancel, +3 s | 429 | 200 |
| One-slot key, cancel during pings, +3 s | 429 | 200 |
| Cancel during pings, billed | $0.108589 | $0 |
| Delete mid-stream, billed output | 5413 tokens | 197 tokens |
| Spend on the 5 cancel keys | $0.1177520 | $0.0003497 |
| Keepalive cut in pings, +3 s, all 3 routes | 429 | 200 |

Both legs run proxies A and B with 2 uvicorn workers each, sharing one Redis and Postgres, on claude-haiku-5-5. Cases create on A and poll, cancel or delete on B. The before leg reuses cases 1 to 7 from the last run at this base commit. The [gist](https://gist.github.com/mateo-berri/d81dfb60197c61f0a137246990d6b51a) has the scripts, the 393 KB prompt and both legs' raw output

<details>
<summary>Run steps (README.md). Cases 6 and 8 boot with `config_keepalive.yaml`, the rest with `config_plain.yaml`. Local paths are placeholders, and `lib.zsh` with the helpers every case calls is in the gist</summary>

```
Run one leg (LEG is head or base):
1. Check the tree: `git -C <tree> status --porcelain` is empty and `git -C <tree> rev-parse HEAD` is the expected sha
2. `redis-server --port <RP> --save '' --appendonly no` in the background
3. `zsh $QA/boot.zsh <LEG> plain <PA>` in the background, and the same for B with <PB>
4. Wait until `curl -s http://127.0.0.1:<port>/health/liveliness` answers on both
5. `zsh $QA/cases.zsh <LEG> plain`
6. Stop both proxies, boot both again with `keepalive` instead of `plain`, wait for liveliness
7. `zsh $QA/cases.zsh <LEG> keepalive`, which runs case 6 and then case 8
8. `zsh $QA/cases.zsh <LEG> spend`
9. Stop both proxies and redis
```

</details>

<details>
<summary>boot.zsh and the after leg's env.zsh, where dotenv-get reads one value from a .env file. The before leg's env.zsh differs only in its tree (base), ports (RP=25646, PA=28675, PB=27636) and database (qa_bg_cancel_base)</summary>

<details>
<summary>mask.py, short.txt and long.txt</summary>

```
# mask.py
import os, re, sys
secrets = [v for v in (os.environ.get(k) for k in ("LITELLM_MASTER_KEY", "QA_KEY", "ONE_SLOT_KEY", "ANTHROPIC_API_KEY")) if v]
def mask(s):
    return "sk-..." + s[-4:]
for line in sys.stdin:
    for v in secrets:
        line = line.replace(v, mask(v))
    line = re.sub(r"sk-(?!\.\.\.)[A-Za-z0-9_\-]{6,}", lambda m: mask(m.group(0)), line)
    line = re.sub(r"postgres(ql)?://[^\s\"']+", "postgresql://<masked>", line)
    sys.stdout.write(line)
    sys.stdout.flush()

# short.txt
Write a 300 word story about a lighthouse.

# long.txt
Write a 1500 word story about a lighthouse.
```

issue.title: fix(anthropic)!: keep thinking disabled, display, between_tools, and effort on /v1/messages to OpenAI
issue.body:
Anthropic `/v1/messages` requests to an OpenAI model now keep the client's thinking controls. Before this, `disabled`, `display`, `between_tools`, and effort without thinking never reached OpenAI, so the model reasoned at its default effort and returned no thinking text

<details>
<summary>Original</summary>

## TLDR

Problem this solves:

- `thinking: disabled` still reasoned at medium effort on OpenAI
- `display: summarized` never returned any thinking text
- `between_tools` and a bare `output_config.effort` were dropped

How it solves it:

- `disabled` maps to `reasoning.effort: none`, or the model's lowest listed level when it has no off switch
- `display` summarized or updates asks for `reasoning.summary: auto`, omitted asks for none
- `between_tools` thinks, with a summary, only after tool results
- `output_config.effort` alone maps to `reasoning.effort` on mapped models that reason by default
- `drop_params` drops an unconfirmed `none`, an unlisted effort, and a summary OpenAI refuses
- The chat route to OpenAI maps them the same way

## User Flow

Before: a developer using Claude Code or `/v1/messages` with an OpenAI model through LiteLLM sees no thinking and cannot turn reasoning off or tune effort

1. They start Claude Code with `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://localhost:4000` and `--model claude-opus-5-5`, which the proxy maps to an OpenAI model
2. They ask a math question and press ctrl+o. The transcript shows an empty `✻ Thinking…` line
3. They send POST http://localhost:4000/v1/messages with `"thinking": {"type": "disabled"}` and get 200, but `x-litellm-response-cost-reasoning` still shows reasoning spend
4. They send `"output_config": {"effort": "max"}` with no thinking, and OpenAI still reasons at its default effort

After: Claude Code shows the model's thinking, and the thinking controls reach OpenAI

1. In Claude Code, the same question shows a `∴` thinking summary above the answer in the ctrl+o transcript
2. The `thinking: disabled` request has no thinking block and no reasoning spend
3. `effort: max` reasons longer than `effort: low`, and `between_tools` thinks only after a tool result

## Type

🐛 Bug Fix

<details>
<summary>Decisions</summary>

1. `disabled` maps to `reasoning.effort: none`. A model whose cost map row lists its effort levels without `none` (gpt-5, gpt-5-mini, gpt-6.1-sol) gets the lowest level it lists, `minimal` or `low`, with or without `drop_params`, since OpenAI answers 400 to `none` there and that level is the closest the model comes to off. `minimal` counts only when the row or the deployment's `model_info` confirms it, with `supports_minimal_reasoning_effort` or a level list, because o3 refuses it, so an o3 deployment that declares only `supports_none_reasoning_effort: false` gets `low`. Only `disabled` and a first-turn `between_tools` take this mapping, and a client's own `effort: none` follows Decision 7. A reasoning model whose row lists no levels (o3, o4-mini, the codex rows) still gets `none`, which `drop_params` drops on both routes when the row does not set `supports_none_reasoning_effort`, so it answers 200 at the model's default effort, and OpenAI answers 400 without `drop_params`. Rejected: dropping the off switch on every model without `none`, which kept the medium reasoning this PR fixes, and a litellm 400 for every unflagged row, since some of them may take `none`
2. `disabled` on a model the cost map knows does not reason (gpt-4.1) sends no reasoning on either route, because that model already does what the client asked and OpenAI would reject the param. A model the cost map does not list gets `none` on both routes, whatever `mode` its `model_info` sets, as the chat route on main does. On the bridge the one exception is a name the Responses transformation looks up and finds without `supports_reasoning`, such as a one-segment `openai/` name only the router registered, which gets no reasoning, as on main, because that transformation answers 400 to `reasoning.effort` there
3. `between_tools` is decided per request: when the final user turn, meaning every user message after the last assistant message, holds a `tool_result`, the model is between tool calls and gets `output_config.effort` (default medium, same as adaptive) with summary `auto`, since Anthropic returns the progress updates as summary text there. A `thinking.summary` or `display: omitted` the client set still wins over that `auto`. Any other turn maps like `disabled` when the model's cost map row or the deployment's `model_info` lists its effort levels, and otherwise sends no reasoning, as on main, because a backend litellm knows nothing about may refuse `none`, as reasoning-only models behind OpenRouter do. A deployment whose `model_info` declares `none` gets it, so a backend that refuses the level its own deployment declares answers 400, as `disabled` on the chat route does on main. Rejected: always off, which loses the thinking agents want between tool calls, and always on, which thinks up front against the request. After a tool result this pays for reasoning at that effort, where Anthropic writes short progress notes
4. `display` reuses the chat route's existing rule, now one shared helper: summarized or updates asks for summary `auto`, omitted asks for none and also overrides the opt-in auto summary. For `updates`, Anthropic leaves reasoning empty and shows only short progress notes, and OpenAI has no separate channel for those notes. Kept `auto` because the chat route on main already maps `updates` this way, and Claude Code sends `updates` on every turn, so mapping it like omitted would show its users no thinking at all. Rejected: none like omitted, and `auto` only between tool calls, which would show OpenAI's summary on some turns and nothing on the others. `thinking.summary` still wins over `display`, and an unset `display` keeps today's behavior. OpenAI answers 400 to an organization it has not verified when a request asks for a summary, so under `drop_params` the bridge retries that request once without the summary and logs a warning, and the client gets its answer with no thinking text. Without `drop_params` the 400 reaches the client. Our OpenAI organization is verified, so only mocked tests cover this retry. Rejected: no summary by default, which would undo the `display` fix for every verified organization
5. `output_config.effort` alone becomes `reasoning.effort` and goes through the same normalizer as adaptive thinking's effort. It sends no `reasoning` in four cases. A model whose cost map row sets `default_reasoning_effort: none` (gpt-5.1, gpt-5.2, the gpt-5.4 family) stays off, because Anthropic never starts thinking that the client left out, and reasoning would also make a `temperature` the model accepts answer 400. A model the cost map knows cannot reason (gpt-4.1, gpt-4o) gets nothing for the same reason. An explicit `reasoning_effort`, from the deployment or the caller, wins, since a bare effort would otherwise override it. A model the cost map does not know gets nothing, because litellm cannot tell whether it reasons. Rejected: turning reasoning on in those cases, which made Claude Code with thinking off pay for reasoning tokens, took a deployment pinned at minimal from 19 to about 500 output tokens, and sent `reasoning` on every request to unmapped hosts like OpenRouter. The budget of `enabled` thinking still wins over `output_config.effort`
6. The chat-completions route to OpenAI (taken only with `stop_sequences` or the chat URL flag) now maps `disabled`, `between_tools`, and a bare effort the same way as the bridge, through the same helper, so a request keeps its meaning when the client adds `stop_sequences`. Other providers on that route keep their mapping, because their models' levels and defaults differ and this PR proves only OpenAI. Rejected: leaving that route alone, which kept the bug for every request with `stop_sequences`
7. An effort no reasoning API defines (`turbo`, say), or one the model's row does not list (high on chat-latest, which lists only medium), is dropped under `drop_params` and goes to OpenAI, which answers 400, without it, adaptive and enabled thinking included, like any other unsupported value. A client's own `effort: none`, adaptive or bare, is one of these on a model whose row lists levels without it (gpt-5-mini) and, as `disabled` is in Decision 1, on a reasoning row that lists none and does not set `supports_none_reasoning_effort` (o3). Rejected: passing it through under `drop_params`, which answered 400 on a request the client asked litellm to clean up
8. Thinking the client sets, `disabled` and `between_tools` included, wins over a deployment's pinned `reasoning_effort`, as adaptive thinking already does on main, because the client asked for that turn. A bare effort does not, per Decision 5. An effort Decision 7 drops, or a `disabled` Decision 1 drops on o3, also keeps the pin out on both routes, so the model answers at its default effort
9. The levels and flags Decisions 1, 3 and 5 read, and the bridge's unlisted-effort check in Decision 7, come from the loaded cost map row (bundled or remote) overlaid with the deployment's own `model_info`. The router also writes every deployment's `model_info` under the backend model's name, so reading by name let one deployment that declares `none` make a sibling that declares nothing send `none`, a 400 on a backend that refuses it. A call with no router deployment keeps the by-name lookup, `register_model` entries included. The OpenAI Responses transformation's own `none` check still reads by name, as a direct `/v1/responses` call does on main, so beside a sibling that declares `supports_none_reasoning_effort: false`, `disabled` and a first-turn `between_tools` answer a litellm 400 without `drop_params` and send no reasoning with it. That shared lookup is older than this PR. Rejected: the by-name lookup for deployments, which shares one deployment's flags with every other deployment of the same model

</details>

## Caveats (if any)

<!-- caveats round 4 of 4 -->

### Medium

- Without `drop_params`, some 200s now answer 400, Anthropic SDK clients included
  - `disabled` on o3, whose row does not confirm `none`, pinned effort included, and `disabled` or first-turn `between_tools` on gpt-5.5-pro
  - `between_tools` after a tool result with a `temperature` other than 1 on gpt-5.4-mini, which Anthropic also refuses
  - `output_config.effort` the model's row does not list or confirm, like high on chat-latest or `none` on gpt-5-mini and o3
  - `disabled` or first-turn `between_tools` beside a sibling deployment that declares `supports_none_reasoning_effort: false`, as `/v1/responses` does on main
  - Claude Code gets `drop_params` from the proxy, and a deployment's fallbacks answer
- `disabled` to an `openai/` deployment the cost map does not list sends `none`, so a backend that requires reasoning answers 400, `drop_params` included, as do `effort: none` after a tool result there and a level `model_info` declares that the backend refuses, like `minimal` on o3
- With `drop_params`, `disabled` and a client's `effort: none` are dropped on o3, o4-mini, and the codex rows, which do not confirm `none`, so they answer at their default effort
- On the bridge, `disabled` and `between_tools` now win over a pinned or caller-sent `reasoning_effort`, as on the chat route (Decision 8)
- `display: updates` and `between_tools` after a tool result pay for OpenAI's full reasoning, not Anthropic's short progress notes
- An unverified OpenAI organization waits on one refused request per summary ask, a retry only mocked tests prove

### Low

- Other providers on the chat route still ignore `between_tools` and a bare effort
- `display` or `summary` with `between_tools` is honored, where Anthropic answers 400
- No caveats round ran on the fixes after round 4

</details>

issue.title: fix(vertex_ai)!: keep anyOf branches next to type and map const to enum
issue.body:
Tool schemas that put `type` and `anyOf` on the same node did not work on Vertex and Gemini, because we kept the type and threw the branches away. An MCP tool can send exactly that shape, so the whole request failed with a 400 and the customer could not use those tools

Now the branches survive. Fields sitting next to `anyOf` move into each branch, since Vertex only accepts `anyOf` alone on a node, and `const` becomes a one-value `enum` because Vertex rejects `const`. The tool schema the caller sent is left as it was

<details>
<summary>Original</summary>

## TLDR

Problem this solves:

- A tool schema with `type` plus `anyOf` lost its branches on Vertex and Gemini
- Vertex then answered 400 for the whole request
- `const` was dropped, so the model could send any value

How it solves it:

- Keep every `anyOf` branch and copy the fields beside it into each branch
- Turn `const` into a one-value `enum`, and add the type when it is missing
- Keep a `required` name only where that branch defines the property
- Clear empty strings and non-string values from enums, which Vertex answers 400 for

Intentional product change: these schemas now reach Vertex with their branches and `const` values, so the model gets stricter rules than before

## User Flow

Before: a developer whose MCP tool schema has `type` next to `anyOf` gets a 400 and the model never calls the tool

1. They send POST https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions for a Vertex Gemini model, with a tool whose `items` has `"type": ["object", "null"]`, an `anyOf` of `const` names, and `"required": ["name"]`
2. The response is 400 with "required properties are specified but schema properties are empty"
3. The same request to a Claude model on the same proxy returns 200 with a `retrieve` tool call

After: the same request comes back 200 with a tool call that uses an allowed value

1. They send the same POST https://litellm-domain/v1/chat/completions with the same tool
2. The response is 200 with a `retrieve` tool call, for example `{"capabilities":[{"name":"People"}]}`
3. The same request to a Claude model on the same proxy still returns 200 with a `retrieve` tool call

## Linear ticket

Resolves LIT-9924

Both legs ran the same way, with `--num_workers 2`, a local Postgres, and real calls to Vertex, the Gemini API, and Anthropic. Only the commit differs. The client is curl because the customer's application sends plain API requests

## Type

🐛 Bug Fix

<details>
<summary>Decisions</summary>

- Scope. The ticket names a type list plus `anyOf`, but a plain `type: object` or a one-item list next to `anyOf` gives the same 400, so all of them take the same path
- `required`. It is the union of the parent's and the branch's names, kept only when that branch defines the property. Vertex answers 400 for a name with no property, so dropping it is the only form Vertex accepts. The alternative was to make up an empty property, which tells the model something the schema never said
- A field on both the parent and a branch. The branch wins, since it is the narrower rule
- Fields next to `anyOf`. Vertex takes `anyOf` alone on a node, so `enum`, `pattern`, `nullable`, and the like move into every branch instead of being lost
- Empty strings in enums. They become null inside `anyOf` too, as they already do elsewhere. Without this a `const: ""` or a moved enum turned a 200 into a 400
- Non-string values in a string enum. They are dropped, and the enum goes away if none are left. No string can match them, so the schema means the same. The alternative was to turn them into strings, which offers the model a value the caller never allowed
- A typed branch keeps its own type. A `number` parent with an `integer` branch stays `integer`, and a branch that matches none of the listed types stays as sent
- An untyped branch is copied once per listed type, and primitive types do not take object or array fields. A `null` copy is removed by the existing null handling, which marks the other branches nullable
- `const`. It becomes a one-value `enum` on every node and fills in `type` when none is set. It wins over an `enum` beside it. An object or list `const` stays dropped as it is today, because a Vertex enum cannot hold one
- No base PR. #43362 handles scalar constraints on type arrays and #41717 handles root object unions, which are different shapes
- #40004 makes the same empty-enum change under `anyOf`. This PR needs it for the case above, so #40004 closes as a duplicate when this merges
- #40415 turns `const` into `enum` for response schemas in a separate pass and does not keep the branches, so it stays separate

</details>

## Final Attestation

issue.title: fix(bedrock): forward output_config.effort to Converse Claude on /v1/messages without a thinking block
issue.body:
## Handwritten 1-3 sentence description

<details>
<summary>Original</summary>

## TLDR

Problem this solves:

- `/v1/messages` to Converse Claude dropped `output_config.effort` without `thinking`
- Structured output ran at the default effort, while Bedrock Invoke sent it

How it solves it:

- The effort part of `output_config` now goes to Converse Claude on its own
- Under `drop_params`, an effort the model can't take is dropped

Intentional product change: without `thinking` or `drop_params`, an effort Converse Claude can't take now gets a 400 instead of a 200 that ignored it

## User Flow

Before: a developer asking a Bedrock Converse Claude deployment for structured output at a set effort gets an answer at the default effort, with no error

1. They send POST http://localhost:4000/v1/messages to a Converse Claude model with `"output_config": {"effort": "medium", "format": {"type": "json_schema", ...}}` and no `thinking`
2. They get 200 with JSON, but the effort never reached Bedrock, so `"effort": "bogus"` also gets 200, while Invoke gives 400

After: the same request reaches Bedrock with the effort they asked for

1. They send the same POST http://localhost:4000/v1/messages to the Converse Claude model
2. They get 200 with JSON, and `"effort": "bogus"` now gets a 400 that lists the allowed values, like Invoke

## Decisions

<details>
<summary>Choices made and the alternatives</summary>

1. The effort is sent whenever the target is Bedrock Claude, with or without `format`
   - The ticket names `format`, but an effort-only request was dropped the same way
   - Only sending it when `format` is present would leave that half broken
2. `format` stays out of the forwarded `output_config`
   - It already reaches Bedrock as `response_format`, either as native structured output or the JSON tool fallback
   - This is the same split the `thinking` path already uses
   - Without `thinking` only `effort` goes, since other keys like `task_budget` never reached Converse there and Bedrock answers 400 to them
3. A model without effort support follows drop_params
   - With `drop_params` on (global, deployment, or request) the effort is dropped with a warning
   - Without it Bedrock answers 400 (`This model does not support the effort parameter` on Haiku 4.5)
   - Keeping the silent drop was rejected, since that silent 200 is the bug
   - Raising a LiteLLM 400 before calling Bedrock was not chosen, to match the `thinking` path that already lets Bedrock answer
   - The Converse check used to read only the global `drop_params`, so a deployment's `drop_params: true` did not drop the effort, which this fixes
4. Non-Bedrock Claude targets (e.g. OpenRouter) still get no effort without `thinking`
   - They take the effort as `reasoning_effort`, which turns on reasoning for some providers, so it is out of scope here
   - That includes a Bedrock ARN behind another provider like `litellm_proxy`, and a caller that names no provider, since only the `bedrock` provider gets the effort without `thinking`
5. An effort tier the model can't take, or a malformed one, is dropped under drop_params
   - `xhigh` on Sonnet 4.6 with `thinking` got LiteLLM's 400 even with `drop_params` on, and the same check now sees requests without `thinking`
   - Only `effort` is dropped, and with `thinking` the other keys are still sent
   - Clamping to the model's top tier was not chosen, since drop_params drops a value it can't send instead of changing it
   - A value that isn't a string, like `["high"]`, used to crash the Bedrock effort clamp with a 500 when `thinking` was set, and now gets the same 400 or drop
6. An application inference profile ARN with no `base_model` gets the effort as before when `thinking` is set, and without `thinking` only when `drop_params` is off
   - LiteLLM can't tell the model behind the ARN, so Bedrock decides
   - Without `thinking` the effort used to be dropped, so `drop_params` keeps that drop with a warning
   - Converse still sends an ARN's `output_config` as given, so `/v1/chat/completions` is unchanged
   - With `base_model` set in `litellm_params` or `model_info`, the effort is sent and checked against that model like any named one
7. A Claude id the cost map does not list yet takes any effort tier when the map's fallback rule marks it adaptive thinking
   - New Claude models take the effort and the tiers current ones do, so neither `drop_params` nor the tier check drops it, and Bedrock decides
8. The shadow eval logger still sends the effort to the shadow model only with `thinking`
   - It translates the logged request for the logged model and sends the result to another model, so Converse's `output_config` would reach a provider that never got it
   - Translating for the shadow model was not chosen, since the auto-router picks that model at call time

</details>

## Pre-Submission checklist

**Please complete all items before asking a LiteLLM maintainer to review your PR**

- [x] I have added meaningful tests
- [x] The handful of test files covering my change pass locally, e.g. `uv run pytest tests/unit/<your_test_file>.py -v`. Leave the suites (`make test-unit-*`, `make test-unit`) to CI: it finishes in ~15 minutes where a laptop takes an hour or more
- [ ] My PR passes all required CI/CD checks (e.g., lint, schema.d.ts sync check, etc.)
- [x] My PR's scope is as isolated as possible; it only solves 1 specific problem
- [ ] Every automated review on my PR's latest commit has finished, and I have addressed or replied to each of its findings before requesting a maintainer review

Last updated: `14145a88c5`. QA ran on `b81c98e38d`. Changes since QA: the base merge was dropped. Proof remains valid because the PR's own diff is unchanged. Verification: per-file diffs match bar a signature wrap main has, and the tests pass
